source_text: Habitabant, inquit, in illa terra ignea corpora, genera scilicet pestifera. cum dicit "habitabant," animata utique atque uiuentia uult intellegi. sed ne de uerbo calumniari uelle uideamur, adtendamus istos omnes habitatores terrae illius, quemadmodum in quinque genera uiua distribuat. hic infinitae, inquit, tenebrae ex eadem manantes natura inaestimabiles cum propriis fetibus; ultra quas erant aquae caenosae ac turbidae cum suis inhabitatoribus; quarum interius uenti horribiles et uehementes cum suo principe et genitoribus. rursum regio ignea et corruptibilis cum suis ducibus et nationibus. pari more introrsum gens caliginis ac fumi plena. in qua morabatur inmanis princeps omnium et dux habens circa se innumerabiles principes, quorum omnium ipse erat mens atque origo: haeque fuerunt naturae quinque terrae pestiferae. animaduertimus quinque naturas quasi partes unius naturae, quam uocat terram pestiferam. hae sunt autem: tenebrae, aquae,. uenti, ignis. fumus; quas quinque naturas sic ordinat, ut exteriores ceteris sint tenebrae, a quibus numerare incipit. intra tenebras aquas constituit; intra aquas uentos; intra uentos ignem; intra ignem fumum. et habebant istae quinque naturae sua quaeque genera inhabitatorum suorum, quae nihilominus quinque sunt. quaero namque, utrum unum genus habitantium fuerit in omnibus quinque naturis, an diuersa genera, sicut naturae ipsae diuersae sunt. diuersa fuisse respondent et de aliis libris ita docent, quod tenebrae serpentes habuerunt; aquae natantes, sicut sunt pisces; uenti uolantes, sicut sunt aues; ignis quadrupedes, sicuti sunt equi, leones et cetera huiusmodi; fumus bipedes, sicuti sunt homines.
thought_title: The five natures and their inhabitants in the land of darkness
orientation: Augustine is quoting and analyzing Mani's description of the land of darkness, which Mani divides into five natures—darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke—each with its own kind of inhabitants.
pass_a_gloss: They were dwelling, he says, in that fiery land [as] bodies, [that is] pestilential kinds. When he says "they were dwelling," [he] wants [them] to be understood [as] animate at any rate and living. But lest we may seem to want to quibble about [the] word, let us attend [to] all those inhabitants of that land, [in] what manner he distributes [them] into five living kinds. Here [are] infinite, he says, darknesses flowing from the same nature [and] immeasurable with [their] own offspring; beyond which were muddy and turbid waters with their [own] inhabitants; [and] within these [were] horrible and violent winds with their [own] prince and parents. Again [there was] a fiery and corruptible region with its [own] leaders and nations. In like manner within [was] a nation full of darkness and smoke. In which was dwelling [the] monstrous prince of all and leader having around himself innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was [the] mind and origin: and these were [the] five natures of [the] pestilential land. We have noticed [the] five natures [as] parts, as it were, of one nature, which he calls [the] pestilential land. These are moreover: darknesses, waters, winds, fire, smoke; which five natures he so arranges, that [the] darknesses are [the] outermost [relative] to [the] rest, from which he begins to count. Within [the] darknesses he places [the] waters; within [the] waters [the] winds; within [the] winds [the] fire; within [the] fire [the] smoke. And those five natures had each their own kinds of their [own] inhabitants, which are nonetheless five. For I ask, whether [there] was one kind of [those] dwelling in all [the] five natures, or different kinds, just as [the] natures themselves are different. They answer [that they] were different and [they] teach so from other books, that [the] darknesses had serpents; [the] waters [had] swimming [creatures], just as are fishes; [the] winds [had] flying [creatures], just as are birds; [the] fire [had] four-footed [creatures], just as are horses, lions and [the] rest of this kind; [the] smoke [had] two-footed [creatures], just as are humans.

choices.why: Keeps the explanatory force of 'scilicet' and the literal sense of 'genera' as kinds, matching the later 'quinque genera'.
Both terms are kept distinct to preserve Augustine's emphasis on Mani's implication of life.
Captures the legalistic sense of 'calumniari' as raising a petty objection.

choices.english: the immense prince of all and leader
choices.why: Keeps both titles 'princeps' and 'dux' distinct, as Mani uses both for the ruler of the land of darkness.
rejected: the huge prince and leader of all
the monstrous prince of all and commander

choices.why: Literal rendering of both nouns, preserving the claim that the prince is the source of thought and being for the other princes.

choices.term: haeque fuerunt naturae quinque terrae pestiferae
choices.english: and these were the five natures of the pestilential land
choices.why: Keeps the summary force of 'fuerunt' and the genitive relation to the pestilential land.
rejected: and these were the five natures of the pestilential earth

pass_b_english: In that fiery land, he says, dwelt bodies—that is, pestilential kinds. When he says “dwelt,” he certainly wants us to understand them as animate and living. But so that I do not seem to quibble over a word, let us look at how he distributes all those inhabitants of that land into five living kinds. Here, he says, were infinite darknesses, flowing from the same nature, immeasurable, with their own offspring; beyond them were muddy and turbulent waters with their own inhabitants; within these were horrible and violent winds with their prince and parents. Again, a fiery and corruptible region with its own leaders and nations. In the same manner, further inward, a race full of gloom and smoke, in which dwelt the immense prince of all and leader, having around him innumerable princes, of all of whom he himself was the mind and origin. And these were the five natures of the pestilential land.

We notice five natures as parts of one nature, which he calls the pestilential land. These are darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke. He arranges these five natures so that darkness is outermost, from which he begins to count. Within the darkness he places the waters; within the waters, the winds; within the winds, fire; within the fire, smoke. And these five natures each had their own kinds of inhabitants, which are likewise five. For I ask whether there was one kind of inhabitant in all five natures, or different kinds, just as the natures themselves are different. They answer that they were different, and they teach from other books that the darkness had serpents; the waters had swimming creatures, such as fish; the winds had flying creatures, such as birds; the fire had quadrupeds, such as horses, lions, and others of this sort; the smoke had bipeds, such as human beings.

last_rejected.quote: In that fiery land, he says, dwelt bodies—that is, pestilential kinds
last_rejected.source_quote: Habitabant, inquit, in illa terra ignea corpora, genera scilicet pestifera
last_rejected.why: Latin 'ignea' modifies 'corpora,' not 'terra'; 'in illa terra' is where they dwelt. English makes land fiery, not bodies.
last_rejected.fix: In that land, he says, dwelt fiery bodies—that is, pestilential kinds.
last_rejected.ruling: 'terra ignea' naturally reads as 'fiery land'; 'ignea' modifying 'corpora' is possible but not required.

last_rejected.quote: We notice five natures as parts of one nature
last_rejected.source_quote: animaduertimus quinque naturas quasi partes unius naturae
last_rejected.why: Missing 'quasi' ('as if,' 'as it were'); English states as fact what Latin presents as Mani's apparent view.
last_rejected.fix: We notice five natures as if parts of one nature
last_rejected.ruling: 'quasi' is lightly hedging; 'as parts' adequately conveys the comparison without distortion.

last_rejected.quote: They answer that they were different
last_rejected.why: Subject unclear; Latin 'respondent' refers to Manichaeans generally, but 'they' in English could mislead. More importantly, 'et de aliis libris ita docent' is omitted—'and from other books they so teach.'
last_rejected.fix: They answer that they were different, and from other books they so teach
last_rejected.ruling: 'They answer...and they teach from other books' renders 'respondent...et de aliis libris ita docent' adequately.

last_rejected.quote: They answer that they were different, and they teach from other books that
last_rejected.source_quote: et de aliis libris ita docent
last_rejected.why: English adds 'and they teach from other books that' but omits 'ita' ('so,' 'thus'), weakening the claim that other books confirm this same arrangement.
last_rejected.fix: and from other books they so teach
last_rejected.ruling: 'ita' is a connective adverb; 'that' clause naturally implies 'thus/so taught,' no meaning lost.
